stories.title: New 'Maths Camera' to Catch Speeding Cars on the BKE
stories.headline_kid: Traffic police are testing a clever new way to catch speedsters on the Bukit Timah Expressway — by doing some quick maths!
summary: The Traffic Police have started testing a brand-new speed-catching system on the Bukit Timah Expressway (BKE). It's called EASE, which stands for Expressway Average Speed Enforcement.

Here's how it works: cameras are placed at the start and end of a stretch of road. They record when a car enters and when it leaves, then work out the car's average speed using the distance travelled and the time taken — just like a maths word problem your teacher might give you!

This is different from the usual speed camera, which only checks your speed at one exact spot. With EASE, you can't simply slow down for the camera and then speed up right after — the system catches your speed over the whole stretch.

During this trial period, no tickets will be given out yet. But once it's fully switched on, cars that go over the average speed limit could be fined. The police say speeding is one of the biggest causes of road accidents in Singapore, so this new system is all about keeping everyone on the road safer.

lenses.me: If your family drives along the BKE, you might notice the car keeping a steadier speed now instead of rushing then braking.
lenses.family: Parents who drive will need to watch their speed the whole way through the zone, not just at one camera.
lenses.friends: Classmates whose parents drive them to school along the BKE will benefit from safer, more careful driving.
lenses.nation: It's part of Singapore's bigger effort to reduce road accidents and keep expressways safe for everyone.
lenses.world: Many countries already use this 'average speed' camera trick — Singapore is now catching up with this global road-safety idea.

compo_words.example: The new cameras can detect cars that are travelling too fast.

stories.title: Facebook and Instagram May Get Stricter Rules for Kids and Teens Everywhere
stories.headline_kid: After a big court case in America, Instagram and Facebook's parent company might add stronger safety rules for young users all over the world — including Singapore.
summary: Meta, the company that owns Facebook and Instagram, recently agreed to a huge settlement in a court case in the United States. The case was about young people being harmed by things they saw or experienced on social media.

As part of the deal, Meta agreed to add stronger age checks and safety features to protect teenagers in America. Experts now think Meta may bring these same protections to other countries too, because it would be easier for the company to use one set of rules everywhere.

This matters for Singapore because many primary and secondary school students use apps like Instagram. If Meta rolls out these changes here, kids might see more warnings, more limits on who can message them, or restrictions on certain content depending on their age.
Experts also say this could push other apps like TikTok or Snapchat to make similar changes, since companies often copy each other once one makes a big safety move.

lenses.me: You might see new age checks or safety pop-ups if you use Instagram or Facebook in future.
lenses.family: Parents may get better tools to see and control what their children can access on these apps.
lenses.friends: Classmates who use social media might need to prove their age or face new limits on chatting with strangers.
lenses.nation: This fits with Singapore's own rules under the Online Safety Act, which already push tech companies to protect young users here.
lenses.world: If Meta changes its rules globally, it could set a new standard that other tech giants feel pressured to follow.

compo_words.example: The app plans to restrict certain features for younger users.

stories.title: Singapore Sends Help as Nepal Flood Deaths Pass 600
stories.headline_kid: Singapore is giving money to help flood victims in Nepal, where a huge wall of mud and water has now killed more than 600 people.
summary: A few days ago, a giant mass of ice, rock, mud and water crashed down from the Himalayan mountains and swept through villages on the border of Nepal and Tibet, in China. It happened after a glacier — a giant block of ice — collapsed high up in the mountains.

The numbers keep getting worse. More than 600 people have died, and the number of people still missing has now shot up past 2,400. Rescue workers are wading through thick mud to search for survivors, and helicopters have been pulling people to safety from flooded valleys.

To help, the Singapore government announced it will give US$100,000 (about S$127,000) as starter money for the Singapore Red Cross's fundraising campaign. This 'seed money' is meant to kickstart donations from the public, so more help can reach families who lost their homes.

The Red Cross says the disaster has left about 93,000 people affected and in great need, with many people badly shaken by what they experienced. Rescue teams briefly had to pause their work when a lake formed by the landslide threatened to overflow, but they have since resumed searching for survivors.

lenses.me: You could ask your parents about donating some pocket money to the Singapore Red Cross appeal to help affected families.
lenses.family: Your family might consider giving to the fundraiser, just like Singapore's government has done.
lenses.friends: Your school might organise a small fundraising activity, like many schools do after big disasters.
lenses.nation: This shows how Singapore helps its neighbours in the region during tough times, even though the disaster happened far away.
lenses.world: It highlights how melting glaciers and mountain disasters can suddenly put thousands of lives at risk, especially as our climate changes.

stories.title: Cambodia Shuts Down Over 700 Scam Centres
stories.headline_kid: Cambodia has shut down more than 700 buildings used to run online scams, and some Singaporeans were among those caught up in it.
summary: Cambodia's government announced that it has shut down more than 700 compounds — groups of buildings — that were being used to run online scams. Some of these places were like scam 'factories', where workers were forced to trick people online into losing their money.
More than 3,400 suspects were arrested. They came from 29 different countries, including China, Vietnam, Australia, and yes — Singapore too. They are now waiting to go to trial.

You may have heard grown-ups talk about scams — like fake messages asking for bank details, or strangers online promising to double your money. These scam compounds are often behind such tricks, targeting victims across many countries, including here in Singapore.

This crackdown is a reminder of why it's important never to click on suspicious links, share personal information, or trust strangers online who promise quick riches — even adults can be fooled by clever scammers.

lenses.me: It's a good reminder to never click on strange links or talk to strangers online who ask for money or personal details.
lenses.family: Your parents should stay alert to messages promising 'easy money' or fake investments, which often trace back to scam compounds like these.
lenses.friends: You and your friends can talk about how to spot a scam message if you ever come across one on your devices.
lenses.nation: Singapore works with police in other countries to catch scammers who target Singaporeans from abroad.
lenses.world: This shows how countries are teaming up to fight cybercrime, since scam networks often cross many borders at once.

stories.title: From Being Left Out of PE to Flying Across the Court for Singapore
stories.headline_kid: Meet Nur Sabrina Suhaimi — once excluded from PE lessons, now she's Singapore's only female national wheelchair rugby player, crashing into opponents on the court!
summary: Nur Sabrina Suhaimi has a rare condition called Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, which slowly weakens her muscles over time. She needs a cane and a leg brace just to walk short distances.

When she was younger, she was often left out of PE lessons because of her condition. But instead of giving up on sport, she found a game where her condition didn't hold her back at all — wheelchair rugby.

Wheelchair rugby used to be nicknamed 'murderball' because it is such a rough, fast-paced sport. Players in special rugby wheelchairs crash into each other while trying to score, making it one of the most physical sports around. Today, Nur Sabrina is Singapore's only female national player in this exciting sport.
Her journey shows that having a disability doesn't stop someone from becoming a strong, competitive athlete — it can even lead them somewhere they never expected.

lenses.me: Her story shows that everyone deserves a fair chance to try different sports, no matter their ability.
lenses.family: It's a reminder to encourage family members with different abilities to find activities where they can truly shine.
lenses.friends: You could think about ways to include classmates with disabilities in games during PE or recess.
lenses.nation: She represents Singapore in international wheelchair rugby competitions, making the country proud.
lenses.world: Wheelchair rugby is a Paralympic sport played in many countries, showing how sport can be made inclusive for everyone.
